claim: Fgf4 and Fgf8 are expressed in the primitive streak and presomitic mesoderm (PSM) of mouse embryos at the five somite stage.
source: (A, A') Max intensity projection (MIP) of HCR staining of Fgf4 and Fgf8 mRNA expression (A) or Fgf4 only (A') in the PSM of a five somite stage wildtype embryo (dorsal view). PS: primitive streak, PSM: presomitic mesoderm, S: somite.
evidence: Figure 1A shows HCR staining demonstrating Fgf4 and Fgf8 mRNA expression patterns in the PSM at five somite stage.

claim: Fgf4 and Fgf8 are expressed in the PSM of mouse embryos at the 10 somite stage.
source: (B) MIP of 4 parasagittal z-sections (approximately 5 µm each) of HCR staining of Fgf4 and Fgf8 mRNA expression, of a 10 somite stage wildtype embryo (lateral view, mediolateral to the midline).
evidence: Figure 1B shows HCR staining demonstrating Fgf4 and Fgf8 mRNA expression in the PSM at 10 somite stage.

claim: Fgf4 mutants are viable and found at Mendelian ratios at weaning.
source: Whereas Fgf8 mutants do not survive much beyond birth due to kidney agenesis (Perantoni et al., 2005), Fgf4 mutants are viable and found at Mendelian ratios at weaning (n = 18 controls and n = 21 mutants).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed numbers of Fgf4 mutants at weaning consistent with Mendelian ratios, and cites Perantoni et al., 2005 for Fgf8 mutant lethality.

claim: Fgf8 mutants do not survive much beyond birth due to kidney agenesis.
source: Whereas Fgf8 mutants do not survive much beyond birth due to kidney agenesis (Perantoni et al., 2005), Fgf4 mutants are viable and found at Mendelian ratios at weaning (n = 18 controls and n = 21 mutants).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Perantoni et al., 2005.

claim: Fgf8 mutant embryos at E18.5 have all vertebral bodies present and normally patterned.
source: Skeleton preparations of Fgf8 mutant embryos at E18.5 (n = 22) revealed all vertebral bodies were present and normally patterned.
evidence: The manuscript reports skeletal preparation analysis of 22 Fgf8 mutant embryos at E18.5.

claim: Fgf8 mutants display minor cervical and/or lumbar homeotic transformations with incomplete penetrance and expressivity.
source: Fgf8 mutants also presented with minor cervical and/or lumbar homeotic transformations, each with incomplete penetrance and expressivity: small ribs were sometimes present in the most posterior cervical vertebra (8/22, 4 bilateral and 4 unilateral) or on the most anterior lumbar vertebra (8/22, 4 bilateral and 4 unilateral).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed frequencies of homeotic transformations in Fgf8 mutants from skeletal preparations.

claim: Fgf4 mutants display a variety of segmentation defects in the cervical and thoracic vertebrae with 100% penetrance.
source: On the other hand, Fgf4 mutants display a variety of segmentation defects in the cervical and thoracic vertebrae with 100% penetrance (Compare Figure 1D,D' with C).
evidence: The manuscript reports 100% penetrance of vertebral defects in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting skeletal preparation images in Figure 1D,D'.

claim: An average of 7.9 defects occurred per Fgf4 mutant, consisting of hemivertebrae, and misshapen and deleted vertebrae.
source: An average of 7.9 defects occurred per mutant and consisted of hemivertebrae, and misshapen and deleted vertebrae (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of vertebral defects in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting histogram in Figure 1E.

claim: Fgf4 mutants at E10.5 display abnormal Uncx mRNA expression patterns in somites.
source: (F–I) Wholemount in situ hybridization (WISH) detection of Uncx mRNA expression in control and Fgf4 mutants at E10.5 (F, G lateral views, anterior top; G' dorsal view of embryo in G) and at 9–10 somite stage (H, I dorsal view, anterior left); dotted line in F and G marks the anterior boundary of the forelimb (FL).
evidence: Figure 1F-I shows WISH staining of Uncx mRNA in control and Fgf4 mutant embryos, demonstrating abnormal patterns in mutants.

claim: In Fgf4 mutants, abnormal somites with mispatterned Uncx expression occur specifically in future cervical and thoracic somites.
source: Analysis of 19 E9.5 Fgf4 mutants revealed a frequency of irregular Uncx expression specifically in future cervical and thoracic somites with full penetrance (Figure 1F–J).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of 19 E9.5 Fgf4 mutants with quantification shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Posterior to somite 21, the Uncx pattern is normal in Fgf4 mutants.
source: (J) Graph depicting the percentage of abnormal somites scored with a mispatterned Uncx mRNA WISH pattern (F–I) in Fgf4 mutants at the somite position listed on the x-axis. Somites were scored in 26–30 somite stage Fgf4 mutants (n = 19). Note that posterior to somite 21 the Uncx pattern is normal.
evidence: Figure 1J shows quantification of abnormal somites in Fgf4 mutants, with annotation indicating normal pattern posterior to somite 21.

claim: Defective Uncx patterning begins at somite three in Fgf4 mutants at somite stage seven.
source: To examine these rostral somites we scored 20 Fgf4 mutants at somite stage seven and found defective Uncx patterning beginning at somite three in this sample set (black bars, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of 20 Fgf4 mutants at somite stage seven with supporting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A majority of Uncx patterning defects in somite 5 and 6 had apparently corrected by somite stage 25 in Fgf4 mutants.
source: Interestingly, a majority of Uncx patterning defects in somite 5 and 6 had apparently corrected by somite stage 25 (gray bars, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of Uncx defects at different developmental stages, with supporting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Somites that correct their Uncx patterning may account for the relatively low level of rostral vertebral defects at E18.5 in Fgf4 mutants.
source: Hence, these somites partially corrected or regulated their pattern and may account for the relatively low level of rostral vertebral defects at E18.5 (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript infers a relationship between corrected Uncx patterns and vertebral defect distribution based on observed data.

claim: This correction of rostral somite patterning is found in embryos lacking Hes7 expression.
source: This correction of rostral somite patterning is found in embryos lacking Hes7 expression (Bessho, 2001), which, as we show below, is reduced in Fgf4 mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bessho, 2001, and reference to data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: Mesp2 is expressed in the anterior PSM and is required for normal somite segmentation and rostral-caudal somite identity.
source: To determine if these malformed somites were due to an error in segmentation, we examined Mesp2 expression, which occurs in the anterior PSM and is required for normal somite segmentation and rostral-caudal somite identity (Saga et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Saga et al., 1997.

claim: At stages when irregular somites are emerging from Fgf4 mutant PSM, aberrant Mesp2 expression is detected.
source: At the stages when irregular somites are emerging from Fgf4 mutant PSM, we detected aberrant Mesp2 expression, whether we analyzed gene expression by traditional wholemount in situ hybridization (WISH) staining (Figure 1K–L) or by fluorescent HCR analysis (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports detection of aberrant Mesp2 expression in Fgf4 mutants using two different methods, with supporting images in Figures 1K-L and 2A,B.

claim: At 22-24 somite stages, when properly segmented somites are emerging from Fgf4 mutant PSM, Mesp2 expression appears normal.
source: However, at later stages (22–24 somite stages), when properly segmented somites are emerging from Fgf4 mutant PSM, Mesp2 expression appears normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports normal Mesp2 expression at later stages in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fgf4 is expressed throughout the PSM at somite stage 22 through E12.5.
source: However, we detected Fgf4 expression throughout the PSM at somite stage 22 through E12.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,C', E–G').
evidence: The manuscript reports detection of Fgf4 expression at later developmental stages, with supporting images in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: TCre-mediated inactivation of Fgf4 results in loss of Fgf4 expression in the PSM at somite stage 6.
source: Indeed, we detect no Fgf4 expression in the PSM at somite stage 6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,B'), when aberrant somites form, nor at somite stage 24 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,D'), when normal somites form.
evidence: The manuscript reports absence of Fgf4 expression in TCre-mediated mutants at multiple stages, with supporting images in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Fgf4 is required for normal somitogenesis only at early stages.
source: Therefore, we conclude that Fgf4 is expressed within the PSM throughout development, but is required for normal somitogenesis only at early stages.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion based on the observation that Fgf4 is absent throughout development in mutants, but defects only occur at early stages.

claim: When Fgf4 is inactivated early in the caudal embryo, abnormally patterned Mesp2 expression occurs only at early stages, causing vertebral defects in Fgf4 mutants.
source: When Fgf4 is inactivated early, in the caudal embryo, abnormally patterned Mesp2 expression occurs only at these early stages, causing the observed vertebral defects in Fgf4 mutants.
evidence: The manuscript infers a causal relationship between early Mesp2 abnormalities and vertebral defects based on temporal correlation.

claim: Mesp2 expression is normally triggered by activated Notch (NICD) and TBX6 at the determination front in the anterior PSM.
source: Mesp2 expression is normally triggered by activated Notch (NICD) and TBX6 at the determination front in the anterior PSM, where cells fall below a critical threshold of wavefront FGF signaling (Oginuma et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Oginuma et al., 2008.

claim: In Fgf4/Fgf8 double mutants, Mesp2 expression is transiently activated throughout the PSM, which then aberrantly expresses the paraxial mesoderm marker, Meox1.
source: We previously showed that this FGF activity was encoded by Fgf4 or Fgf8; if we inactivated both Fgfs with TCre (Fgf4/Fgf8 double mutant), Mesp2 expression is transiently activated throughout the PSM, which then aberrantly expresses the paraxial mesoderm marker, Meox1 (Naiche et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Naiche et al., 2011, describing previous work by the authors.

claim: Neither the length nor level of expression of Tbx6 and Msgn1 were significantly altered in Fgf4 mutants.
source: Neither the length nor level of expression of Tbx6 and Msgn1 were significantly altered in Fgf4 mutants (Figure 2C,C", D,D", E,F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of Tbx6 and Msgn1 expression in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting data in Figure 2.

claim: The paraxial differentiation marker, Meox1, was not expanded into the PSM in Fgf4 mutants.
source: Consistent with this observation, the paraxial differentiation marker, Meox1, was not expanded into the PSM (Figure 2C' and D'), as occurs in Fgf4/Fgf8 double mutants (Naiche et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript reports Meox1 expression analysis in Fgf4 mutants with supporting images in Figure 2, and cites Naiche et al., 2011 for comparison to double mutants.

claim: Wavefront activity is normal in Fgf4 mutants.
source: Therefore, we conclude that wavefront activity is normal in Fgf4 mutants, an insight consistent with the observation that normal axis extension occurs in these mutants, with no loss of caudal vertebrae (Anderson et al., 2016a).
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion based on gene expression data and cites Anderson et al., 2016a for supporting observation.

claim: Normal wavefront position and signaling in Fgf4 mutants are likely maintained by Fgf8.
source: We surmise that this normal wavefront position and signaling in Fgf4 mutants are likely maintained by Fgf8, which is expressed at normal levels (Figure 3A–C) and is sufficient for maintaining normal expression levels of the FGF target genes, Spry2, Etv4, and Spry4 (Figure 3D–F'''); these FGF targets are silenced in Fgf4/Fgf8 double mutants (Naiche et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript infers Fgf8 compensates for Fgf4 loss based on normal Fgf8 and FGF target gene expression in Fgf4 mutants (Figure 3), and cites Naiche et al., 2011 for comparison to double mutants.

claim: Fgf8 expression levels are normal in Fgf4 mutants.
source: We surmise that this normal wavefront position and signaling in Fgf4 mutants are likely maintained by Fgf8, which is expressed at normal levels (Figure 3A–C)
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of Fgf8 expression in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Fgf4 mutants maintain normal expression levels of the FGF target genes Spry2, Etv4, and Spry4.
source: We surmise that this normal wavefront position and signaling in Fgf4 mutants are likely maintained by Fgf8, which is expressed at normal levels (Figure 3A–C) and is sufficient for maintaining normal expression levels of the FGF target genes, Spry2, Etv4, and Spry4 (Figure 3D–F''')
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of FGF target gene expression in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting data in Figure 3D-F'''.

claim: FGF target genes Spry2, Etv4, and Spry4 are silenced in Fgf4/Fgf8 double mutants.
source: these FGF targets are silenced in Fgf4/Fgf8 double mutants (Naiche et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Naiche et al., 2011.

claim: Neither a change in wavefront activity nor a change in determination front position explains the aberrant pattern of Mesp2 expression in Fgf4 mutants.
source: Therefore, neither a change in wavefront activity nor a change in determination front position explains the aberrant pattern of Mesp2 expression in Fgf4 mutants.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion based on the observation that wavefront markers are normal in Fgf4 mutants.

claim: Overall NICD levels were unchanged between Fgf4 mutants and littermate controls at embryonic stages when somitogenesis was abnormal.
source: Overall NICD levels were unchanged between Fgf4 mutants and littermate controls at the embryonic stages when somitogenesis was abnormal (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of NICD levels in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting data in Figure 4A.

claim: Two to three distinct stripes of NICD are observed along the anterior-posterior axis in both mutant and littermate control PSM at early somite stages.
source: At these stages, we always observed two to three distinct stripes of NICD along the anterior-posterior axis in both mutant and littermate control PSM (Figure 4B–C), demonstrating the oscillatory nature of Notch activation (Bone et al., 2014; Morimoto et al., 2005; Huppert et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript reports observation of NICD stripes in both control and mutant embryos, with supporting images in Figure 4B-C and citations to Bone et al., 2014; Morimoto et al., 2005; Huppert et al., 2005.

claim: Mutant oscillatory stripes of NICD are less ordered compared to controls.
source: However, mutant oscillatory stripes of NICD were always less ordered, compared to controls.
evidence: The manuscript reports qualitative assessment of NICD stripe organization in mutants versus controls.

claim: In controls, cells medial-lateral to each other have similar levels of activated NICD, whereas in mutants, this organization is less distinct.
source: This was more evident when the relative intensities of NICD immunostaining signals were modeled using Imaris software. In controls, cells medial-lateral to each other had similar levels of activated NICD, whereas in mutants, this organization was less distinct (Figure 4B'–C').
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of NICD patterns using Imaris modeling, with supporting images in Figure 4B'-C'.

claim: The blurred NICD pattern in Fgf4 mutants occurs in the anterior PSM, where NICD activates Mesp2 expression at the determination front.
source: Importantly, this blurred pattern occurred in the anterior PSM, where NICD activates Mesp2 expression at the determination front (Figure 4B'–C', brackets).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial localization of NICD pattern abnormalities in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting images in Figure 4B'-C'.

claim: Lfng encodes a glycosyltransferase that represses Notch signaling in the PSM.
source: Lfng encodes a glycosyltransferase that represses Notch signaling in the PSM (Ferjentsik et al., 2009; Dale et al., 2003; Okubo et al., 2012), possibly via glycosylation of DLL1 and/or DLL3 (Panin et al., 2002; Serth et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ferjentsik et al., 2009; Dale et al., 2003; Okubo et al., 2012; Panin et al., 2002; Serth et al., 2015.

claim: Hes7 is a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that is essential for repression of a number of Notch target genes.
source: Hes7 is a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that is essential for repression of a number of Notch target genes (Niwa et al., 2007; Bessho, 2001; Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Niwa et al., 2007; Bessho, 2001; Chen et al., 2005.

claim: Hes7 and Lfng are targets of activated Notch and their expression oscillates.
source: Hes7 and Lfng are themselves targets of activated Notch and therefore their expression oscillates (Niwa et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Niwa et al., 2011.

claim: Disruption of either Hes7 or Lfng causes uncoordinated Notch signaling in the PSM.
source: Disruption of either gene causes uncoordinated Notch signaling in the PSM (Niwa et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Niwa et al., 2011.

claim: Oscillatory expression of Hes7 and Lfng are apparent in both Fgf4 mutants and littermate controls.
source: Although oscillatory expression of Hes7 and Lfng are apparent in both Fgf4 mutants and littermate controls (Figure 4D–E''), the mutant patterns are indistinct, similar to the mutant NICD pattern (Figure 4D–E'').
evidence: The manuscript reports observation of oscillatory Hes7 and Lfng expression in both controls and mutants, with supporting images in Figure 4D-E''.

claim: The mutant patterns of Hes7 and Lfng are indistinct, similar to the mutant NICD pattern.
source: Although oscillatory expression of Hes7 and Lfng are apparent in both Fgf4 mutants and littermate controls (Figure 4D–E''), the mutant patterns are indistinct, similar to the mutant NICD pattern (Figure 4D–E'').
evidence: The manuscript reports qualitative assessment of Hes7 and Lfng patterns in mutants, with supporting images in Figure 4D-E''.

claim: Lfng expression is particularly disordered in the anterior PSM of Fgf4 mutants.
source: Lfng expression is particularly disordered in the anterior PSM (Figure 4E' and E''; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), where both NICD and Mesp2 also show aberrant patterning (Figure 4C,C' and Figures 1L and 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial localization of Lfng pattern abnormalities in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting images in Figure 4E', E'' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hes7 expression is disordered in the mutant PSM at early somite stages.
source: Hes7 expression is likewise disordered in the mutant PSM at these stages (Figure 4E,E'').
evidence: The manuscript reports observation of disordered Hes7 expression in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting images in Figure 4E,E''.

claim: The aberrant Mesp2 pattern in Fgf4 mutants can be explained by loss of coordinated Notch signaling at the differentiation front.
source: Together, these data suggest the aberrant Mesp2 pattern in Fgf4 mutants can be explained by loss of coordinated Notch signaling at the differentiation front.
evidence: The manuscript infers a causal relationship between disordered Notch signaling and aberrant Mesp2 expression based on observed patterns.

claim: The transcriptional repressor encoded by Hes7 is considered to be a fundamental pacemaker of the segmentation clock that controls somitogenesis.
source: The transcriptional repressor encoded by Hes7 is considered to be a fundamental pacemaker of the segmentation clock that controls somitogenesis (Kageyama et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kageyama et al., 2012.

claim: Hes7 is within the Hes/Her class of transcriptional repressors that are the only oscillating clock genes conserved among mouse, chicken, and zebrafish.
source: Hes7 is within the Hes/Her class of transcriptional repressors that are the only oscillating clock genes conserved among mouse, chicken, and zebrafish (Krol et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Krol et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations that accelerate HES7 production will accelerate the tempo of the segmentation clock in the mouse.
source: In the mouse, mutations that accelerate HES7 production will accelerate the tempo of the segmentation clock (Harima et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Harima et al., 2013.

claim: HES7 directly represses Lfng transcription.
source: Moreover, HES7 directly represses Lfng transcription (Chen et al., 2005) and is required for normal Lfng oscillations within the PSM (Ferjentsik et al., 2009; Bessho, 2001; Dale et al., 2003; Okubo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2005; Ferjentsik et al., 2009; Bessho, 2001; Dale et al., 2003; Okubo et al., 2012.

claim: HES7 is required for normal Lfng oscillations within the PSM.
source: Moreover, HES7 directly represses Lfng transcription (Chen et al., 2005) and is required for normal Lfng oscillations within the PSM (Ferjentsik et al., 2009; Bessho, 2001; Dale et al., 2003; Okubo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ferjentsik et al., 2009; Bessho, 2001; Dale et al., 2003; Okubo et al., 2012.

claim: Defective Hes7 expression could account for the abnormal NICD and Mesp2 patterning in Fgf4 mutants, possibly by causing aberrations in Lfng expression.
source: Therefore, defective Hes7 expression could account for the abnormal NICD and Mesp2 patterning in Fgf4 mutants, possibly by causing aberrations in Lfng expression.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a hypothesis based on known relationships between Hes7, Lfng, and Notch signaling.

claim: Analysis of Hes7 mRNA in Fgf4 mutants at 5-6 somite stages using conventional WISH revealed a reduced and aberrant expression pattern.
source: Analysis of Hes7 mRNA in Fgf4 mutants at 5–6 somite stages, using conventional WISH, revealed a reduced and aberrant expression pattern in Fgf4 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports WISH analysis of Hes7 expression in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting images in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the E8.5 PSM, there are two to three Hes7 expression stripes in both controls and Fgf4 mutants.
source: However, in the E8.5 PSM, when aberrant Notch signaling occurs in Fgf4 mutants, there are two to three Hes7 expression stripes in both controls and Fgf4 mutants (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports observation of Hes7 stripes in both controls and mutants at E8.5, with supporting images in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Control embryos are distributed nearly equally between each phase of Hes7 oscillation at E8.5.
source: Control embryos are distributed nearly equally between each phase (Figure 5G) as is the case for Hes7 expression in older embryos (Bessho, 2001; Bessho et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript reports distribution of control embryos across oscillation phases, with supporting data in Figure 5G and citations to Bessho, 2001; Bessho et al., 2003.

claim: Fgf4 mutants can be allocated within all three phases of Hes7 oscillation, with most found in oscillation phase II.
source: However, in our assessment, we allocated Fgf4 mutants within all three phases (Figure 5D–F), with most found in oscillation phase II (Figure 5G).
evidence: The manuscript reports distribution of Fgf4 mutants across oscillation phases, with supporting data in Figure 5D-G.

claim: PSM-specific Hes7 expression is reduced in Fgf4 mutants to 51.8% of that expressed in litter-mate controls.
source: PSM-specific Hes7 expression is reduced in Fgf4 mutants to 51.8% of that expressed in litter-mate controls (Figure 5H).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of Hes7 expression in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting data in Figure 5H.

claim: The reduction in Hes7 expression in Fgf4 mutants is not due to the difference in phase allocation between Fgf4 mutants and littermate controls.
source: A comparison between mutant and control Hes7 expression levels within each phase reveals that the reduction in Fgf4 mutants is not due to the difference in phase allocation between Fgf4 mutants and littermate controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports phase-specific analysis of Hes7 expression, with supporting data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: After the 22 somite stage, there is no significant difference in Hes7 PSM expression levels between Fgf4 mutants and controls.
source: Moreover, after the 22 somite stage, when forming somites are normally segmented in mutants (Figure 1J), there is no significant difference in Hes7 PSM expression levels between Fgf4 mutants and controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of Hes7 expression at later stages, with supporting data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: A reduction of Hes7 expression may account for the defective segmentation during rostral somitogenesis in Fgf4 mutants.
source: Therefore, we conclude that a reduction of Hes7 expression may account for the defective segmentation during rostral somitogenesis in Fgf4 mutants.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion based on the temporal correlation between reduced Hes7 expression and segmentation defects.

claim: In control embryos, the distribution of Hes7 expression spots is significantly skewed towards higher intensity quintiles compared to Fgf4 mutants.
source: In controls, the lowest intensity quintile (blue) contains the most spots (40%) and each higher-intensity group contains 10% fewer spots (Figure 6A, white bars in C). The distribution of spots in the Fgf4 mutant, compared to controls, is significantly skewed towards the lowest quintile at the cost of higher-level expression spots (Figure 6B, black bars in C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of Hes7 expression intensity distribution using spot modeling, with supporting data in Figure 6A-C.

claim: In control embryos, each stripe of Hes7 expression contains a concentric gradient of signal intensity with highest expression at the center and lowest expression at the outside.
source: In control embryos, each stripe of Hes7 expression contains a concentric gradient of signal intensity with highest expression at the center (white spots) and lowest expression at the outside (blue spots) (Figure 6A,D).
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial analysis of Hes7 expression intensity within stripes, with supporting images in Figure 6A,D.

claim: Fgf4 mutants maintain some concentric organization of Hes7 expression, but with greater variability of expression between neighboring cells.
source: Fgf4 mutants maintain some of this concentric organization, but with a greater variability of expression between neighboring cells, the boundaries between groups is less clear (Figure 6B,E).
evidence: The manuscript reports qualitative assessment of Hes7 expression organization in Fgf4 mutants, with supporting images in Figure 6B,E.

claim: The trough between peaks of Hes7 expression is more shallow in Fgf4 mutants and contains more higher-intensity spots than littermate controls.
source: In particular the trough between peaks of Hes7 expression is more shallow, and contains more higher-intensity spots (mostly second quintile, green) than littermate controls (Figure 6D' and E').
evidence: The manuscript reports spatial analysis of Hes7 expression in the trough region, with supporting images in Figure 6D',E'.

claim: Transcription of Hes7 is reduced in the posterior PSM and is more widespread, extending into the trough between Hes7 mRNA peaks in the Fgf4 mutant.
source: To determine if this indicated a failure to repress Hes7 transcription in these regions, we performed HCR using a probe that hybridizes to the Hes7 intronic sequences, and therefore specific to newly transcribed pre-mRNA. This analysis revealed that transcription of Hes7 is reduced in the posterior PSM and is more widespread, extending into the trough between Hes7 mRNA peaks in the Fgf4 mutant (white brackets in Figure 6F', G').
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of Hes7 transcription using intronic probes, with supporting images in Figure 6F',G'.

claim: FGF4 is required to maintain Hes7 transcription in the PSM above a threshold required for normal patterns of Notch gene oscillation.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that FGF4 is required to maintain Hes7 transcription in the PSM above a threshold required for normal patterns of Notch gene oscillation.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a hypothesis based on observed Hes7 expression patterns in Fgf4 mutants.

claim: The reduced level of HES7 in Fgf4 mutants is insufficient to fully autorepress its own expression, resulting in an aberrant pattern of expression.
source: The reduced level of HES7 in Fgf4 mutants is insufficient to fully autorepress its own expression, resulting in an aberrant pattern of expression.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanism based on observed Hes7 expression patterns and known autorepression.

claim: About 50% of Hes7 heterozygotes have defective lower thoracic vertebrae with a frequency of 2.8 defects per animal.
source: About 50% of our Hes7 heterozygotes had defective lower thoracic vertebrae with a frequency of 2.8 defects per animal.
evidence: The manuscript reports observed vertebral defects in Hes7 heterozygotes.

claim: Littermate Fgf4 mutants display vertebral defects with complete penetrance, with an average of 7.7 defects per animal.
source: In littermate Fgf4 mutants, vertebral defects were completely penetrant, with an average of 7.7 defects per animal, a frequency similar to that of progeny in our original genetic cross (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed vertebral defects in Fgf4 mutants from the genetic cross with Hes7 heterozygotes.

claim: Compound Fgf4/Hes7 mutants display 25 defects per animal, a frequency significantly greater than littermate Fgf4 mutants (3-fold greater, p<0.005) or Hes7 heterozygotes (9-fold greater, p<0.001).
source: However, compound Fgf4/Hes7 mutants displayed a large set of defects with 25 defects per animal (Figure 7C–E), a frequency significantly greater than littermate Fgf4 mutants (3-fold greater, p<0.005) or Hes7 heterozygotes (9-fold greater, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of vertebral defects in compound mutants with statistical analysis, with supporting data in Figure 7C-E.

claim: The vertebral defects in compound Fgf4/Hes7 mutants indicate a synergistic, as opposed to additive, effect of loss of one Hes7 allele in the Fgf4 mutant.
source: These data indicate a synergistic, as opposed to additive, effect of loss of one Hes7 allele in the Fgf4/Hes7 compound mutant.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the observed defect frequencies as indicating synergy rather than additivity.

claim: Vertebral defects in compound Fgf8/Hes7 mutants are not synergistic but are clearly the Hes7 heterozygous defects added to the relatively mild Fgf8 defects.
source: Vertebral defects in compound Fgf8/Hes7 mutants were not synergistic (four defects per animal) but were clearly the Hes7 heterozygous defects added to the relatively mild Fgf8 defects (1.8 defects per animal, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of vertebral defects in Fgf8/Hes7 compound mutants, with supporting data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no genetic interaction between Fgf8 and Hes7.
source: Therefore, we demonstrate that the relationship between Hes7 and Fgf4 is unique in that there is no genetic interaction between Fgf8 and Hes7.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion based on the additive rather than synergistic defects in Fgf8/Hes7 compound mutants.

claim: A reduction in Hes7 expression correlates with the severity of vertebral defects within each genotype from the Fgf4/Hes7 mutant littermates.
source: We then examined levels and spatial patterns of Hes7 mRNA expression in each genotype from the Fgf4/Hes7 mutant littermates, specifically within a volumetric model of the Tbx6 expression domain, as we had in Fgf4 mutants (Figures 5 and 6). We observed a reduction in Hes7 expression that correlated with the severity of vertebral defects within each genotype (Figure 7E).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of Hes7 expression in multiple genotypes, with supporting data in Figure 7E.

claim: Hes7 null heterozygotes have only a 19% reduction in Hes7 expression.
source: Hes7 null heterozygotes had only a 19% reduction in expression, presumably because a loss of HES7 auto-repression results in enhanced transcription from the remaining wildtype allele.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of Hes7 expression in Hes7 heterozygotes and proposes a mechanism for the modest reduction.

claim: Compound Fgf4/Hes7 mutants have an 80% reduction in Hes7 expression.
source: Such compensatory upregulation fails in compound Fgf4/Hes7 mutants because we observed an 80% Hes7 reduction to occur in these embryos (Figure 7E).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of Hes7 expression in compound Fgf4/Hes7 mutants, with supporting data in Figure 7E.

claim: Oscillations appear relatively normal if Hes7 levels are reduced 19% (in Hes7 heterozygotes) but are disordered with a 33% reduction (in Fgf4 mutants).
source: Analysis of intensity-colored spot models of PSMs of these genotypes suggests a threshold effect of Hes7 levels on oscillatory gene expression (Figure 7F–I). Oscillations appear relatively normal if Hes7 levels are reduced 19% (in Hes7 heterozygotes, Figure 7G) but are disordered with a 33% reduction (in Fgf4 mutants, Figure 7H).
evidence: The manuscript reports qualitative assessment of oscillation patterns in different genotypes using spot models, with supporting images in Figure 7F-I.

claim: The synergistic 80% reduction of Hes7 in compound Fgf4/Hes7 mutants causes a severe dampening of oscillatory gene expression.
source: The synergistic 80% reduction of Hes7 that occurs in compound Fgf4/Hes7 mutants causes a severe dampening of oscillatory gene expression (Figure 7I).
evidence: The manuscript reports qualitative assessment of oscillation patterns in compound mutants using spot models, with supporting images in Figure 7I.

claim: The vertebral defects in compound Fgf4/Hes7 mutants are not as extreme as occurs in Hes7 null homozygotes, indicating that the reduced level of Hes7 supports limited patterning during segmentation.
source: The resulting vertebral defects, though relatively severe (Figure 7A–D), are not as extreme as occurs in Hes7 null homozygotes (Bessho, 2001), indicating that this reduced level of Hes7 supports limited patterning during segmentation.
evidence: The manuscript compares the severity of defects in compound mutants to Hes7 null homozygotes, citing Bessho, 2001.

claim: FGF4 acts to maintain Hes7 above a necessary threshold for normal somitogenesis.
source: Together, our data support our hypothesis that FGF4 acts to maintain Hes7 above a necessary threshold for normal somitogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion based on the genetic interaction data between Fgf4 and Hes7.

claim: In Fgf4 mutants, a reduction in Hes7 levels leads to abnormal patterns of activated Notch.
source: In Fgf4 mutants, a reduction in Hes7 levels, leads to abnormal patterns of activated Notch.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a causal chain based on observed correlations between Hes7 levels and Notch patterns.

claim: Abnormal Notch oscillations initiate Mesp2 unevenly in the anterior PSM leading to improperly shaped somites and subsequently, malformed vertebrae.
source: Abnormal Notch oscillations initiate Mesp2 unevenly in the anterior PSM leading to improperly shaped somites and subsequently, malformed vertebrae.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a causal chain linking abnormal Notch oscillations to vertebral defects based on observed patterns.

claim: Fgf4 mutants resemble human congenital scoliosis (CS).
source: Our mutants model human Segmentation Defects of the Vertebrae (SDV); Fgf4 mutants resemble CS and the synergistic phenotype resulting from the additional removal of one Hes7 copy in these mutants resembles human SCDO.
evidence: The manuscript proposes that Fgf4 mutants model human disease based on phenotypic similarity.

claim: The synergistic phenotype resulting from the additional removal of one Hes7 copy in Fgf4 mutants resembles human spondylocostal dysostosis (SCDO).
source: Our mutants model human Segmentation Defects of the Vertebrae (SDV); Fgf4 mutants resemble CS and the synergistic phenotype resulting from the additional removal of one Hes7 copy in these mutants resembles human SCDO.
evidence: The manuscript proposes that compound Fgf4/Hes7 mutants model human disease based on phenotypic similarity.

claim: CS and SCDO are caused by mutations in Notch signaling components such as HES7, MESP2, and LFNG.
source: Both of these diseases are caused by mutations in Notch signaling components that we find are misexpressed in Fgf4 mutants, such as HES7, MESP2, and LFNG (Eckalbar et al., 2012; Giampietro et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eckalbar et al., 2012; Giampietro et al., 2009.

claim: Gestational hypoxia in mice results in an increase in the severity and penetrance of CS in Notch1, Mesp2, and Hes7 heterozygotes.
source: Sparrow et al found that gestational hypoxia in mice results in an increase in the severity and penetrance of CS in Notch1, Mesp2, and Hes7 heterozygotes (Sparrow et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sparrow et al., 2012.

claim: CS is more severe in children living at high altitudes.
source: Intriguingly, CS is more severe in children living at high altitudes (Hou et al., 2018), suggesting a similar environmental effect may affect human development.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hou et al., 2018.

claim: Hypoxia diminishes FGF signaling components in mice, but expression of Fgf8 is unchanged.
source: In mice, hypoxia was found to diminish FGF signaling components, but expression of Fgf8 was unchanged, and Fgf4 was unexamined (Sparrow et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sparrow et al., 2012.

claim: FGF4 may be part of the system that is responsive to hypoxia-induced environmental insult.
source: Our data suggest that FGF4 may be part of the system that is responsive to this environmental insult.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about FGF4's role in hypoxia response based on observed phenotypic similarities.

claim: Reduced FGF4 activity cannot be the only response to reduced oxygen levels because gestational hypoxia reduces expression of the FGF target gene Spry4 in the PSM, whereas there is no change in expression of Spry4 or other canonical FGF target genes in Fgf4 mutants.
source: However, if this is the case, reduced FGF4 activity cannot be the only response to reduced oxygen levels because gestational hypoxia reduces expression of the FGF target gene Spry4 in the PSM, whereas we found no change in expression in this or other such canonical FGF target genes in Fgf4 mutants.
evidence: The manuscript argues against a simple model based on comparison of gene expression patterns in hypoxia versus Fgf4 mutants.

claim: Hes7 expression is reduced in hypoxia-treated embryos.
source: Rather, as is the case for hypoxia-treated embryos (Sparrow et al., 2012), Hes7 expression is reduced in Fgf4 mutants and we propose that this leads to aberrant segmentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sparrow et al., 2012.

claim: Reduced Hes7 expression in Fgf4 mutants leads to aberrant segmentation.
source: Rather, as is the case for hypoxia-treated embryos (Sparrow et al., 2012), Hes7 expression is reduced in Fgf4 mutants and we propose that this leads to aberrant segmentation.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a causal relationship based on observed correlation between reduced Hes7 and segmentation defects.

claim: HCR allows for quantitative and multiplexed mRNA detection.
source: Because the fluorescent signal intensity corresponds proportionally to the number of mRNA molecules (Trivedi et al., 2018), HCR allows for quantitative and multiplexed mRNA detection (Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Trivedi et al., 2018 and Choi et al., 2018.

claim: A reduction in Hes7 levels, due to heterozygosity or hypomorphic mutations, has been shown to cause vertebral defects.
source: A reduction in Hes7 levels, due to heterozygosity or hypomorphic mutations, has been shown to cause vertebral defects (Sparrow et al., 2012; Fujimuro et al., 2015; Stauber et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sparrow et al., 2012; Fujimuro et al., 2015; Stauber et al., 2009.

claim: Hes7 is generally regulated by FGF signaling.
source: The concept that Hes7 is generally regulated by FGF signaling is supported by numerous studies (Naiche et al., 2011; Niwa et al., 2007; Harima and Kageyama, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Naiche et al., 2011; Niwa et al., 2007; Harima and Kageyama, 2013.

claim: Hes7 may be a direct FGF4 signaling target, possibly through putative ETS binding sites in the Hes7 promoter.
source: Future work will determine whether Hes7 is a direct FGF4 signaling target, possibly through putative ETS binding sites in the Hes7 promoter (González et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about direct regulation and cites González et al., 2013 for the presence of ETS binding sites.

claim: FGF4 may indirectly regulate Hes7 transcription by affecting the activity of TBX6, NICD or MESOGENIN, all shown to regulate Hes7 expression in the PSM.
source: Alternatively, FGF4 may indirectly regulate Hes7 transcription by affecting the activity of TBX6, NICD or MESOGENIN, all shown to regulate Hes7 expression in the PSM (González et al., 2013; Hayashi et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about indirect regulation and cites González et al., 2013; Hayashi et al., 2018 for the role of these factors in Hes7 regulation.

claim: FGF4 signaling may be interfacing with WNT signaling, which has been shown to regulate Hes7.
source: Additionally, it is possible that FGF4 signaling is interfacing with WNT signaling, which also has been shown to regulate Hes7 Aulehla et al., 2008; Dunty et al., 2008; González et al., 2013.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about FGF-WNT interaction and cites Aulehla et al., 2008; Dunty et al., 2008; González et al., 2013 for WNT regulation of Hes7.

claim: FGF4 does not have a primary role on Lfng expression.
source: Given the molecular feedbacks during genetic oscillations in the PSM, we considered whether FGF4 might have a primary role on Lfng expression, whose pattern is abnormal in our mutants. However, we suggest this is not the case, because, although embryos completely lacking Lfng also display aberrant Hes7 oscillations (Niwa et al., 2007; Stauber et al., 2009), overall Hes7 mRNA levels are not reduced (Ferjentsik et al., 2009), unlike the case in our Fgf4 mutants.
evidence: The manuscript argues against a primary role for FGF4 on Lfng based on comparison to Lfng mutants, citing Niwa et al., 2007; Stauber et al., 2009; Ferjentsik et al., 2009.

claim: Embryos completely lacking Lfng display aberrant Hes7 oscillations but overall Hes7 mRNA levels are not reduced.
source: However, we suggest this is not the case, because, although embryos completely lacking Lfng also display aberrant Hes7 oscillations (Niwa et al., 2007; Stauber et al., 2009), overall Hes7 mRNA levels are not reduced (Ferjentsik et al., 2009), unlike the case in our Fgf4 mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Niwa et al., 2007; Stauber et al., 2009; Ferjentsik et al., 2009.

claim: In Fgf4 mutants, Hes7 mRNA levels are reduced during rostral somitogenesis at E8.5 (5-6 somite stages), when defective somitogenesis occurs.
source: We observed that in Fgf4 mutants Hes7 mRNA levels are reduced during rostral somitogenesis at E8.5 (5–6 somite stages), when defective somitogenesis occurs.
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal correlation between reduced Hes7 levels and defective somitogenesis.

claim: At about E9.5 (24-26 somite stages), Hes7 levels are unaffected in Fgf4 mutants, and the embryo is beginning to generate correctly patterned somites.
source: At about E9.5 (24–26 somite stages), Hes7 levels are unaffected, and the Fgf4 mutant embryo is beginning to generate correctly patterned somites that will differentiate into normally patterned vertebrae.
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal correlation between normal Hes7 levels and normal somitogenesis at later stages.

claim: Between E8.5 and E9.5, somites more than double in size in mouse development.
source: Tam, 1981 showed that between these two stages of mouse development, somites more than double in size.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tam, 1981.

claim: An increase in segment size can be due to a slower segmentation clock and/or faster regression of the determination front.
source: Such an increase in segment size can be due to a slower segmentation clock and/or faster regression of the determination front (Oates et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Oates et al., 2012.

claim: The caudal movement of the wavefront does not significantly change between E8.5 and E9.5.
source: Gomez et al., 2008 found that the caudal movement of the wavefront does not significantly change at these stages, suggesting a slowing clock between E8.5 and E9.5.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gomez et al., 2008.

claim: At least 2 and frequently 3 bands of Hes7 expression are observed at the Fgf4-sensitive stages (5-6 somite stages).
source: Consistent with a slower clock, we observed at least 2 and frequently 3 bands of Hes7 expression at the Fgf4-sensitive stages (5–6 somite stages; Figures 4 and 5), but only 1 to 2 bands when Fgf4 loss has no effect on Hes7 expression (24–26 somite stages; Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports observation of Hes7 expression bands at different developmental stages, with supporting images in Figures 4, 5, and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Only 1 to 2 bands of Hes7 expression are observed when Fgf4 loss has no effect on Hes7 expression (24-26 somite stages).
source: Consistent with a slower clock, we observed at least 2 and frequently 3 bands of Hes7 expression at the Fgf4-sensitive stages (5–6 somite stages; Figures 4 and 5), but only 1 to 2 bands when Fgf4 loss has no effect on Hes7 expression (24–26 somite stages; Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports observation of Hes7 expression bands at later developmental stages, with supporting images in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: FGF4 activity is required to maintain Hes7 mRNA levels above a certain threshold when the segmentation clock is faster.
source: Thus, it appears that FGF4 activity is required to maintain Hes7 mRNA levels above a certain threshold when the segmentation clock is faster; when Notch oscillations slow, they may become FGF-independent, or other FGFs may be at play.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a hypothesis based on temporal correlation between clock speed and FGF4 requirement.

claim: When Notch oscillations slow, they may become FGF-independent, or other FGFs may be at play.
source: Thus, it appears that FGF4 activity is required to maintain Hes7 mRNA levels above a certain threshold when the segmentation clock is faster; when Notch oscillations slow, they may become FGF-independent, or other FGFs may be at play.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about mechanisms at later developmental stages.

claim: Embryos with faster segmentation clocks, such as snakes, might have a longer window of FGF4-dependence for normal somitogenesis.
source: If this is the case in all vertebrates, we might expect embryos with faster segmentation clocks, such as snakes (Gomez et al., 2008), to have a longer window of FGF4-dependence for normal somitogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about evolutionary implications and cites Gomez et al., 2008 for snake segmentation clock speed.

claim: FGF4 and FGF8 redundantly encode wavefront activities, preventing PSM differentiation.
source: This study and past work indicate that FGF4 and FGF8 have both shared and unique roles in the vertebrate embryo's posterior growth zone. They redundantly encode wavefront activities, preventing PSM differentiation (Naiche et al., 2011; Boulet and Capecchi, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Naiche et al., 2011; Boulet and Capecchi, 2012.

claim: When FGF4 and FGF8 signal together, they activate downstream canonical FGF target genes, such as Spry2, Spry4, and Etv4.
source: In this capacity, when signaling together, they activate downstream canonical FGF target genes, such as Spry2, Spry4, and Etv4 (Naiche et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Naiche et al., 2011.

claim: The role that FGF4 signals play in maintaining Hes7 mRNA levels cannot be replaced by FGF8.
source: Here, we show the role that FGF4 signals play in maintaining Hes7 mRNA levels cannot be replaced by FGF8.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion based on the genetic interaction data showing synergy between Fgf4 and Hes7 but not Fgf8 and Hes7.

claim: FGFR1 is thought to be the only FGF receptor gene expressed in the PSM.
source: For example, our work argues for a reassessment of FGFR function in the PSM; prior work, in which the same Cre driver used here (TCre) inactivates Fgfr1 (Wahl et al., 2007), thought to be the only FGF receptor gene expressed in the PSM, does not exactly phenocopy the defects due to TCre-mediated loss of either Fgf4 (this study) or Fgf4/Fgf8 (Naiche et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites Wahl et al., 2007 for the view that FGFR1 is the only FGF receptor in the PSM.

claim: TCre-mediated inactivation of Fgfr1 does not exactly phenocopy the defects due to TCre-mediated loss of either Fgf4 or Fgf4/Fgf8.
source: For example, our work argues for a reassessment of FGFR function in the PSM; prior work, in which the same Cre driver used here (TCre) inactivates Fgfr1 (Wahl et al., 2007), thought to be the only FGF receptor gene expressed in the PSM, does not exactly phenocopy the defects due to TCre-mediated loss of either Fgf4 (this study) or Fgf4/Fgf8 (Naiche et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript compares phenotypes across different mutants and cites Wahl et al., 2007 and Naiche et al., 2011.

claim: Somitogenesis predates vertebrate evolution as it occurs in Cephalochordata, the most basal living chordates.
source: Somitogenesis predates vertebrate evolution as it occurs in Cephalochordata, the most basal living chordates (Holland and Onai, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Holland and Onai, 2012.

claim: In both Cephalochordates and Urochordates, the FGF essential for embryonic axis extension is an Fgf8 ortholog.
source: In both Cephalochordates and Urochordates, the FGF essential for embryonic axis extension is an Fgf8 ortholog (Bertrand et al., 2015; Pasini et al., 2012), suggesting that this Fgf ('Fgf8/17/18') may be the ancestral gene in this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bertrand et al., 2015; Pasini et al., 2012.

claim: Fgf8/17/18 may be the ancestral gene in embryonic axis extension.
source: In both Cephalochordates and Urochordates, the FGF essential for embryonic axis extension is an Fgf8 ortholog (Bertrand et al., 2015; Pasini et al., 2012), suggesting that this Fgf ('Fgf8/17/18') may be the ancestral gene in this process.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about evolutionary history based on comparative data, citing Bertrand et al., 2015; Pasini et al., 2012.

claim: Fgf8/17/18 activity in invertebrate chordates does not control gene oscillations as these embryos apparently lack a segmentation clock.
source: However, Fgf8/17/18 activity in these invertebrate chordates does not control gene oscillations as these embryos apparently lack a segmentation clock (Bertrand et al., 2015; Onai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bertrand et al., 2015; Onai et al., 2015.

claim: The recruitment of an Fgf4 role during the evolution of vertebrate axis extension may have coincided with the development of gene oscillations that control somitogenesis.
source: Therefore, we speculate that the recruitment of an Fgf4 role during the evolution of vertebrate axis extension may have coincided with the development of gene oscillations that control somitogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about evolutionary history based on comparative functional data.

claim: Fgf4 is potentially important in a spectrum of human Segmentation Defects of the Vertebrae caused by defective Notch oscillations.
source: Our data indicate that Fgf4 is potentially important in a spectrum of human Segmentation Defects of the Vertebrae caused by defective Notch oscillations.
evidence: The manuscript proposes clinical relevance based on the mouse mutant phenotypes and their similarity to human diseases.
